findings.headline: Six Business Continuity audit findings from 2024/25 remain pending internal auditor follow-up 12 months after their original due dates.
findings.detail: Six audit actions from the 2024/25 Business Continuity audit had original deadlines between 30 June and 30 September 2025. All six remain marked 'IA to Follow-Up' as of 22 September 2026, including training needs assessment and Depot Services BCP testing, neither of which have updates recorded. The IT and Projects BCP was revised in April 2026 but also remains awaiting final follow-up.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to observe how peers address slow audit remediation, as consistently overdue actions could indicate governance or organisational capacity constraints affecting financial management.
findings.figures: Six findings; original due dates 30/06/2025–30/09/2025; current status as at 22 September 2026
findings.quote: IA to Follow-Up

findings.headline: Three audit findings in Revenues and Benefits remain in pending remediation status with deadlines in December 2026 and June 2027.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 audit identified three matters in Revenues and Benefits requiring remediation: empty property quarterly review outputs, quality assurance procedures, and business continuity plan. All are marked as pending remediation as of 22 September 2026, with due dates of 31 December 2026 for the BCP and 30 June 2027 for the other two. Revenue collection is a critical income function for councils.
findings.matters: A lender would care about unresolved audit findings affecting revenue administration, as revenue collection is fundamental to the council's financial resilience and debt service capacity.
findings.figures: Three findings with due dates 31/12/2026 and 30/06/2027
findings.quote: Pending Remediation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: Pension liability of £11.96m carries additional contribution rate of 22.4% plus £699k lump sum following March 2025 revaluation
findings.detail: The council's Local Government Pension Scheme liability stands at £11.96m. The scheme was revalued in March 2025, setting an additional contribution rate of '22.4% plus £699k' for 2025/26. The council contributed £1.95m to the scheme during 2025/26 and recognised a £0.78m charge. This additional rate means the council pays above-standard contributions to offset the pension deficit.
findings.matters: Pension contributions of 22.4% plus fixed costs represent a significant and growing embedded cost in the council's base budget that limits flexibility to redirect spending to emerging priorities
findings.figures: Pension liability £11.96m; additional contribution rate 22.4% plus £699k lump sum; total contributions paid £1.95m; year charge £0.78m
findings.quote: The last valuation took place in March 2025 which set our additional contribution rate at 22.4% plus £699k for the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: Council is funding capital investment through asset sales, having sold Bushloe House in 2025/26 and negotiating swimming pool sale for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council 'concluded the sale of its former offices at Bushloe House in Wigston' during 2025/26 and is 'progressing negotiations for the sale of Oadby swimming pool, with the sale expected in 2026/27.' Capital receipts increased from £1.78m combined (2024/25) to £4.661m combined (2025/26), indicating asset sales are a material funding source. This funding approach is not sustainable long-term without a portfolio of disposable assets.
findings.matters: Dependency on asset sales to fund capital investment indicates weak capital funding from mainstream sources and represents a non-renewable funding strategy that will eventually exhaust the council's asset base
findings.figures: Usable capital receipts (GF) increased from £62k to £1.512m; (HRA) from £1.718m to £3.149m; combined increase £2.881m
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council concluded the sale of its former offices at Bushloe House in Wigston. We have also progressed negotiations for the sale of Oadby swimming pool, with the sale expected in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 59% of planned spend, with HRA capital at 40% of budget
findings.detail: The council budgeted £7.199m for capital investment but spent only £4.220m, creating an underspend of £3.258m (45%). General Fund capital achieved 80% spend (£2.672m of £3.364m budget), but HRA capital performed significantly weaker at 40% (£1.548m of £3.835m budget). This capital underperformance suggests difficulty in delivering planned service improvements and housing maintenance.
findings.matters: Capital underperformance indicates the council may lack delivery capacity for planned investments and could create pressure to extend plans into future years, deferring service improvements
findings.figures: Total capital budget £7.199m, outturn £4.220m (underspend £3.258m); GF £3.364m budgeted, £2.672m spent (£692k under); HRA £3.835m budgeted, £1.548m spent (£2.287m under)
findings.quote: For 2025/26 our revenue budgets totalled £7.7 million and our capital investment programme £7.199 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reserves fell from £1.675m to £925k following £774k allocation to contingency reserve
findings.detail: The HRA reserve opened at £1.675m and closed at £925k, representing a £750k reduction. Although the HRA recorded a 'budget surplus of £24k', the council moved £774k into a contingency reserve to cushion against housing cost pressures, leaving the main HRA reserve at £925k (15% of gross HRA income). This drawdown reduces the HRA's capacity to absorb unexpected pressures in housing maintenance or voids.
findings.matters: Housing reserves are being depleted to create contingency buffers, reducing resilience against inflation in repairs and maintenance costs and rental income shortfalls
findings.figures: HRA reserve opening £1.675m, closing £925k (reduction £750k); £774k transferred to contingency reserve; HRA reserve now 15% of gross income
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the account has a budget surplus of £24k, however, £774k was moved to a contingency reserve, leaving an HRA Reserve balance of £925k as at 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: General Fund reserves increased by only £35k to £1.457m, with council acknowledging reserves remain below prudent levels
findings.detail: Despite receiving £1.3m more contribution from reserves than budgeted (an adverse outturn variance), the General Fund reserve increased only marginally from £1.422m to £1.457m. The council states explicitly: 'We know that we need to build our level of General Fund reserves to remain healthy and resilient in the future and this is flagged in the CIPFA Financial Resilience Index and other benchmarking data when our reserves performance is compared to other districts.' This signals the council recognises its reserves are constrained for a district authority.
findings.matters: Low reserves limit the council's ability to respond to unexpected pressures, revenue shortfalls, or service demands and indicate financial fragility relative to peer councils
findings.figures: General Fund reserve: opening £1.422m, closing £1.457m (increase £35k); £1.307m net contribution to reserves in-year versus £323k budgeted
findings.quote: We know that we need to build our level of General Fund reserves to remain healthy and resilient in the future and this is flagged in the CIPFA Financial Resilience Index and other benchmarking data when our reserves performance is compared to other districts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan projects budget gaps and reserve depletion across five-year period despite 2026/27 balanced budget
findings.detail: The council's MTFP approved in February 2026 shows 'budget gaps each year' and deficits throughout the forecast period that will deplete reserves. The council has addressed 2025/26 and 2026/27 through 'Substantial savings...made under the sustainability program', but the narrative acknowledges the council has not resolved the structural gap. The budget has contracted from £8.5m (2010/11) to £7.7m (2025/26), a 9% reduction.
findings.matters: Year-on-year dependency on savings programmes to close budget gaps indicates the council lacks structural solutions to its funding shortfall and sustainability is dependent on continued savings delivery
findings.figures: Budget reduced from £8.5m in 2010/11 to £7.7m in 2025/26; MTFP projects deficits across 5-year forecast period
findings.quote: The current medium term financial plan looks ahead to the forthcoming five-year period and projects deficits over the course of the 5-year forecast resulting in the General fund reserve decreasing over the life of the MTFP.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audited Financial Report (2025/26) & Annual Governance Statement (2025/26)
findings.headline: Homelessness costs overran by £1.07m in 2025/26, the largest single adverse variance in the revenue budget
findings.detail: The council reported an adverse variance of £1,068,865 on homelessness, driven by demand-led pressures from cost-of-living inflation. The narrative attributes this to 'unprecedented demands around homelessness support and costs', indicating an emerging cost pressure that councils cannot control. This single line item accounted for the majority of the council's net adverse variances across all services.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are demand-driven and outside council control, creating unfunded spending pressures that compress other services and will recur each year unless underlying cost-of-living pressures ease
findings.figures: £1,068,865 adverse variance on homelessness
findings.quote: The impact of inflation on the cost of living creates more demand for our services and is creating unprecedented demands around homelessness support and costs.

findings.headline: Value for money arrangements assessed as satisfactory; no significant weaknesses in governance, financial sustainability, or economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.detail: The auditor assessed the council's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness across three NAO Code criteria: governance, financial sustainability, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. No significant weaknesses were identified in any area. The VFM opinion is unqualified.
findings.matters: A satisfactory VFM assessment confirms the council has put proper arrangements in place for resource management and service delivery, with no significant operational or strategic governance failures identified.
findings.figures: No significant weaknesses identified across all three VFM criteria
findings.quote: We are satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.headline: Collection fund evidence delays persist into 2025/26 audit; no internal timeline improvement implemented since prior year.
findings.detail: Delays in obtaining collection fund supporting documentation (reliefs, debtors, creditors) have continued from prior-year audit into 2025/26. The team responsible sits outside the main finance function. Auditor recommendation for internal timelines has not been implemented.
findings.matters: Recurring collection fund delays signal potential disconnection between finance and revenues/benefits functions at year-end close; they also risk masking errors in a material balance and affect audit efficiency.
findings.figures: Issue identified in both 2024/25 and 2025/26 audits; affects collection fund debtors, creditors, and reliefs
findings.quote: Throughout the audit we experienced significant delays in obtaining collection fund related evidence. Specifically, transaction listings for reliefs, debtors and creditors

findings.headline: S151 officer approving manual journals due to small finance team; segregation of duties risk remains despite prior audit recommendation.
findings.detail: The S151 officer continues to approve manual journal entries — a segregation of duty weakness. Management notes that with only three officers authorized to approve journals, concurrent absence makes alternative coverage unavoidable. Auditor has kept the prior-year recommendation open as best practice would exclude the S151 officer from this role.
findings.matters: S151 officer journal approval creates both a segregation of duty control gap and concentration of financial controls in a single individual; a structural constraint driven by team size that represents an ongoing control weakness.
findings.figures: 3 officers authorized to approve manual journals; S151 officer among those approving
findings.quote: There are only three officers that can approve manual journals, and the possibility that both of the two non-S151 officers are on annual leave or sick leave at the same time will always exist.

findings.headline: General ledger system (Integra 2) rated amber for security management; privileged user access control deficiency unresolved from prior year.
findings.detail: The Integra 2 general ledger received an amber IT general control rating for security management (non-significant deficiencies identified). Prior-year findings regarding elevated access rights for finance team members remain unresolved despite recommendation. Enhanced audit procedures for journal testing were performed to mitigate management override risk.
findings.matters: A general ledger system with amber-rated security and unresolved privileged access issues creates inherent risk of unauthorized or erroneous transactions; persistence of elevated access despite prior audit findings raises questions about control implementation priority.
findings.figures: Integra 2 overall IT general control rating: Amber; security management: Amber
findings.quote: one member of the finance team who had elevated access rights, not commensurate of their role. Users with administrative privileges at application level can bypass internal control mechanisms and may compromise the integrity of financial data

findings.headline: Unpresented cheques totalling £20,554 dated before 2023 remain uncleared and unwritten off; issue persists from prior year.
findings.detail: Long-standing unpresented cheques continue to sit on the balance sheet. Originally £18,322 for cheques dated 2010–2021, the balance has now grown to £20,554 for items dated pre-2023. Despite prior-year audit recommendation, the council has not written these off. The auditor has kept the recommendation open for review in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Multi-year unpresented cheques indicate either unreconciled clearing anomalies or unresolved payments; their persistence raises control questions about bank reconciliation discipline, year-end close processes, and management's follow-up on audit findings.
findings.figures: Unpresented cheques £20,554 (pre-2023); originally £18,322 (2010–2021)
findings.quote: We noted, from review of the bank reconciliation, that the Council have recurring unpresented cheques totalling £18,322. The cheques are dated between 2010 and 2021. Our audit work in the cash and cash equivalent confirmed that these were not written off during 2025/26. Cheques dated prior to 2023 total £20,554.

findings.headline: Five undisclosed directorships held by three councillors identified during audit; one councillor's interest register not updated since 2023.
findings.detail: Testing of the register of interests identified five undisclosed directorships held by three councillors. Additionally, one councillor's online register has not been updated since 2023 (noted to be due to serious illness). Both issues create risk of undetected conflicts of interest and undisclosed related-party transactions in accounts preparation.
findings.matters: Undisclosed directorships and stale interest registers undermine governance controls for identifying conflicts of interest; material where the council holds significant contracts with third parties in which councillors have an interest.
findings.figures: 5 undisclosed directorships; 3 councillors involved; 1 register last updated 2023
findings.quote: Audit procedures have identified five undisclosed directorships for three councillors, on review of the individual register of interests.

findings.headline: Minimum revenue provision applies 2% rate against 4% required by statutory guidance; MRP understated by £48,776.
findings.detail: The council continues to apply 2% MRP under the capital financing requirement method, while statutory guidance prescribes 4%. Management defends this as prudent, but the auditor has kept the recommendation open. This policy choice understates the annual revenue provision by approximately £48,776 and affects reported reserves, persisting from prior year.
findings.matters: Ongoing divergence from statutory MRP guidance directly affects the true cost of borrowing and adequacy of revenue reserves; a persistent policy choice despite audit recommendation raises questions about management's interpretation of prudence and compliance.
findings.figures: MRP understated by £48,776 at 2% vs required 4% rate
findings.quote: Per statutory guidance authorities should use 4% of the closing capital financing requirement to calculate MRP. The Council applies 2%, as a result we have estimated that MRP is understated by £48,776.

findings.headline: Gross expenditure decreased from £16.239m to £15.761m; audit materiality recalculated accordingly.
findings.detail: The council's gross expenditure fell materially year-on-year, requiring recalculation of audit materiality from £897,000 to £858,000. The paper does not explain whether this £478,000 (2.9%) reduction is structural (e.g. service reduction) or temporary (e.g. timing of grants or capital activity), leaving the underlying driver unclear for peers and lenders watching.
findings.matters: Material expenditure swings signal either service reductions or funding changes that affect future financial capacity; a finance director or lender would want to understand whether this is structural or one-off.
findings.figures: Prior year expenditure £16.239m; current year £15.761m; decrease £0.478m (2.9%); materiality adjusted from £897,000 to £858,000
findings.quote: Materiality has been updated to £858,000 based on 2.4% of draft gross expenditure as the expenditure has decreased to £15,761m (PY: £16,239m).

findings.headline: Unmodified audit opinion issued despite five prior-year recommendations remaining outstanding.
findings.detail: The audit opinion is unmodified and only one trivial adjustment to the financial statements was identified. However, five of twelve prior-year audit recommendations remain unresolved, including segregation of duties in journal approval, IT privileged access controls on Integra 2, long-standing unpresented cheques, MRP policy non-compliance, and collection fund evidence delays.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion combined with persistent unresolved control weaknesses signals where audit materiality sits relative to the control environment — important context for assessing financial statement reliability and control maturity.
findings.figures: Unmodified opinion; 1 trivial adjustment; 5 of 12 prior-year recommendations unresolved
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be unmodified.

findings.headline: Open audit agreed actions from previous audits are being tracked and followed up.
findings.detail: The report confirms that all agreed actions arising from previous audit work are being actively followed up, with a separate tracking report (Appendix 2) listing all open agreed actions. This demonstrates the council is managing its response to audit recommendations.
findings.matters: Whether a council implements audit recommendations reflects governance discipline and management of control deficiencies. Peer councils and lenders track follow-through to assess how seriously audit findings are treated.
findings.figures: Specific agreed actions not detailed in this report; tracked in Appendix 2
findings.quote: We will follow up all agreed actions. A report (Appendix 2) showing all open agreed actions has been included for Members information.

findings.headline: Council Tax and Benefits audit completed with Low Substantial assurance, Business Rates with Mid Substantial.
findings.detail: Three audits have been concluded since the last committee meeting. Council Tax and Benefits received a Low Substantial assurance rating and Business Rates a Mid Substantial rating. Substantial ratings indicate controls are operating effectively with only minor exceptions. These cover two of the council's primary revenue-generating functions.
findings.matters: A lender examining control risk wants to see effective controls over tax collection and benefit administration—both critical to council financial stability. Audit assessment of these core functions directly affects perceived control soundness.
findings.figures: Three audits finalized: Taxi Licensing (Advisory), Council Tax and Benefits (Low Substantial), Business Rates (Mid Substantial)
findings.quote: Council Tax and Benefits – Low Substantial - Business Rates – Mid Substantial

findings.headline: Revenues and Benefits core financial systems (Council Tax and Business Rates) received substantial assurance opinions with no priority 1 or 2 recommendations; prior audit action completed
findings.detail: Audits of both Council Tax and Benefits and Business Rates issued 'Substantial' assurance opinions, meaning 'A sound system of governance, risk management and control exists, with internal controls operating effectively and being consistently applied.' Both received Medium risk ratings. Only Priority 3 (routine) recommendations were made: 2 for Council Tax and Benefits, 1 for Business Rates. Testing confirmed that 'an action from a previous revenues and benefits audit concerning a review of outstanding debt is now complete.'
findings.matters: Strong audit assurance on core revenue collection systems is fundamental to a lender's assessment of the council's financial resilience and ability to service debt; completed prior actions demonstrate management follow-through
findings.figures: Council Tax and Benefits: Substantial opinion, Medium risk, 0 Priority 1/2 recommendations, 2 Priority 3; Business Rates: Substantial opinion, Medium risk, 0 Priority 1/2 recommendations, 1 Priority 3
findings.quote: A sound system of governance, risk management and control exists, with internal controls operating effectively and being consistently applied to support the achievement of objectives in the area audited.

findings.headline: Taxi licensing service operates with one full-time and one part-time officer handling approximately 1400 applications annually, creating business continuity and fraud risk
findings.detail: The audit noted that 'The current taxi licensing team has one full-time officer and one part-time officer with approximately 1400 applications processed annually. This potentially risks business continuity in the event of absences, puts staff wellbeing at risk and increases the risk of fraud with officers approving their own work.'
findings.matters: Severe understaffing creates service continuity risk and operational vulnerability; inability to cover absences increases fraud risk when separation of duties cannot be maintained
findings.figures: 1 full-time officer; 1 part-time officer; 1400 applications processed annually
findings.quote: The current taxi licensing team has one full-time officer and one part-time officer with approximately 1400 applications processed annually. This potentially risks business continuity in the event of absences, puts staff wellbeing at risk and increases the risk of fraud with officers approving their own work.

findings.headline: Taxi licensing data protection breaches identified: DBS certificates stored without safeguarding rationale, retention policies inconsistent and in breach of GDPR
findings.detail: The audit found a DBS certificate had been stored without clear reason, breaching DBS guidance and UKGDPR rights. It also identified that retention policies for taxi licensing are inconsistent: the Document Retention Policy states two years' retention while the Licensing PN states six years from application or expiry. The audit concluded this creates 'uncertainty over how long records should be kept' and increases the risk of GDPR breach.
findings.matters: Data protection and regulatory compliance breaches expose the council to enforcement action from the ICO and carry reputational risk; a lender needs visibility of material compliance failures
findings.figures: Document Retention Policy V3.1 (June 2023) states two years; Licensing PN specifies six years from date of application and expiry date
findings.quote: Inconsistent retention policies and unclear guidance on storing safeguarding records increase the risk that the Council may keep personal data in breach of an individuals' UKGDPR rights.

findings.headline: Taxi licensing advisory audit identified control gaps in application processing with 42.86% of sampled applications missing required checks
findings.detail: An advisory audit of taxi licensing (1 January to 30 April 2026) found that of 14 applications reviewed, 6 completed applications had missing checks on required documentation and 5 had inconsistent use of checks in the IDOX Uniform system. The audit concluded this 'lack of standardised process is due to the lack of written procedures, and could lead to applications being processed incorrectly, sensitive data being mishandled, licences being suspended without proper authorisation, and the issuing of licences without sufficient documents.'
findings.matters: Inconsistent controls in licensing processes create exposure to fraud, mishandling of sensitive information, and unauthorised decisions; they also indicate broader governance weaknesses in how the council manages critical services
findings.figures: 42.86% of 14 applications had missing checks; 35.71% had inconsistent checks
findings.quote: lack of standardised process with an unreliable audit trail. The lack of standardised process is due to the lack of written procedures, and could lead to applications being processed incorrectly, sensitive data being mishandled, licences being suspended without proper authorisation, and the issuing of licences without sufficient documents.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation paused by government on 7 September 2026 after decision on two-unitary model but council had budgeted for transition.
findings.detail: The government announced on 16 July 2026 that Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland would be replaced by two unitary councils from 1 April 2028, with Oadby and Wigston moving to a unitary covering Leicester City, parts of Blaby, Charnwood and Harborough. However, on 7 September 2026 the government paused LGR for review. The council had earmarked LGR funds in its 2026/27 budget and medium-term financial plan; residual risks remain around transition governance, resource capacity and financial systems.
findings.matters: Councils in LGR geographies face significant budget, staffing and system risks during transition; a pause creates uncertainty but the council's prior budgeting suggests preparedness; for lenders, transition risk affects borrowing strategy and repayment capacity.
findings.figures: LGR decision paused 7 September 2026; vesting day originally 1 April 2028; council earmarked LGR funds in budget
findings.quote: On 16 July 2026, the Government (selecting from options proposed by the Councils) decided that, from 1 April 2028, Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland councils would be replaced by two new unitary councils... In line with this announcement, reorganisation across Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland is currently paused for review.

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion anticipated with no significant weaknesses in arrangements and no statutory powers used.
findings.detail: The audit anticipates issuing an unqualified opinion on the council's financial statements in October 2026 following the Audit Committee meeting on 7 October 2026. Draft financial statements were of reasonable standard and supported by detailed working papers; no significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements were identified and no statutory recommendations, Public Interest Reports or court applications were issued.
findings.matters: An unqualified opinion with no audit concerns indicates clean financial statements and effective governance; lenders and peer councils track audit opinions as a signal of financial and governance health.
findings.figures: Unqualified opinion to be issued October 2026; no audit powers used
findings.quote: We anticipate to issue an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements in October 2026. We have nothing to report in respect of the above matters.

findings.headline: Three Amber governance improvement recommendations: counter-fraud not embedded, late budget amendments limited scrutiny, risk reporting clarity reduced.
findings.detail: Counter-fraud: the Anti-Fraud and Corruption Policy was not reviewed on schedule, no annual counter-fraud report presented to Members, and fraud baseline assessment remained incomplete. Budget amendments: significant changes proposed shortly before committee consideration limited analysis time before initial consideration. Risk reporting: Q3 and Q4 reports removed target scores and RAG ratings; Audit Committee members raised concerns about readability and a Member clarification from April 2026 was not evidenced as addressed.
findings.matters: Governance process weaknesses create risk that fraud, budget decisions or strategic risks are not adequately identified or challenged; none reached significant weakness threshold but indicate control gaps requiring attention.
findings.figures: Three improvement recommendations raised (IR1, IR2, IR3)
findings.quote: Whilst we identified no significant weaknesses in governance arrangements, we made improvement recommendations relating to counter-fraud arrangements, significant budget amendments and risk reporting to the Audit Committee.

findings.headline: Members approved lower Council Tax increases and car parking charges than Section 151 Officer proposed, reducing financial headroom but budget remained sustainable.
findings.detail: During the 2026/27 budget process, Members approved amendments to reduce the planned Council Tax increase and freeze car parking charges, contrary to Section 151 Officer advice which was recorded in committee minutes. The Section 151 Officer concluded in the Section 25 report that budget estimates remained robust and prudent, and the audit found no evidence the decision undermined sustainability or deliverability.
findings.matters: Member-elected decisions rejecting finance officer income advice illustrate the political dimension of council budgeting; the budget remaining sustainable despite reduced income signals either sufficient headroom or manageable impact, but also reduced future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Amendments reduced forecast income and financial headroom; final budget remained balanced and robust
findings.quote: Although Members approved amendments to the proposed budget which reduced forecast income and financial headroom, the final budget remained balanced and was assessed as robust and prudent by the Section 151 Officer.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget approved as balanced without requiring General Fund reserves support or additional savings.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget was approved in balance without drawing on General Fund reserves or identifying additional savings. This closes the prior year improvement recommendation that the council needed further income generation or savings schemes; the £2.41m 'savings plan' reported reflected net budget changes rather than unidentified savings requirements.
findings.matters: A balanced budget without reserve support or unidentified savings indicates the council has moved from financial stress to sustainability and demonstrates delivery on prior audit recommendations.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget approved balanced; £2.41m 'savings plan' reflected net budget changes not unidentified savings
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget was approved as balanced without requiring savings or General Fund reserves support. Officers confirmed that the £2.41m "savings plan" reported in the 2026/27 budget reflected net budget changes rather than unidentified savings requirements.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan forecasts surpluses throughout 2026/27 to 2030/31, representing significant improvement on prior year.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan forecasts General Fund surpluses throughout the planning period to 2030/31 with no current known funding gap, a significant turnaround from the prior year when funding gaps were forecast. The improvement reflects favourable changes to government funding, an assumed 2.99% annual Council Tax increase after 2026/27, and no other increases to fees and charges.
findings.matters: Moving from forecast deficits to surpluses signals material improvement in financial sustainability; funding gaps typically trigger service cuts or reserve drawdown so their absence represents a material shift in financial position.
findings.figures: Surpluses forecast throughout 2026/27 to 2030/31; assumed 2.99% annual Council Tax increase after 2026/27
findings.quote: the MTFP forecasts General Fund surpluses throughout the period to 2030/31 and represents a significant improvement on the prior year's forecast, reflecting favourable changes to government funding, an assumed 2.99% annual increase in Council Tax after 2026/27, and no other increases to fees and charges.

findings.headline: Reserve position strengthened during 2025/26 improving financial resilience.
findings.detail: The council's reserves improved during the year, strengthening its financial buffer against future pressures. This represents positive movement in financial flexibility at a time when many councils face reserve pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves are the primary lever councils have when facing unexpected pressures; strengthening reserves signals the council is managing current pressures well and preparing for future uncertainty.
findings.figures: Overall improvement stated but not quantified
findings.quote: The Council's reserve position strengthened during the year, improving financial resilience.

findings.headline: General Fund outturn £0.14m overspend on £7.72m budget despite £1.07m homelessness cost overrun.
findings.detail: The council reported only a small net overspend after offsets elsewhere in 2025/26, demonstrating effective budget control despite significant homelessness pressures from increasing demand for temporary accommodation. Early 2026/27 monitoring indicates performance remains broadly in line with budget.
findings.matters: A small overspend with the homelessness pressure well-identified and offset suggests budget discipline and financial resilience despite external pressures affecting many councils.
findings.figures: General Fund overspend £0.14m against budget of £7.72m; homelessness overspend £1.07m
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the Council reported a General Fund overspend of £0.14m against a budget of £7.72m. The most significant pressure remained homelessness, which overspent by £1.07m due to increasing demand for temporary accommodation and rising costs. This was mostly offset by underspends elsewhere.

findings.headline: LGR uncertainty creating staff retention and recruitment challenges; ringfenced budget allocated
findings.detail: Uncertainty about Local Government Reorganisation is creating staff retention and recruitment challenges, threatening loss of skills and organizational capacity. Implementation planning is paused at government request. A ringfenced budget has been allocated for LGR but scope depends on further government announcements.
findings.matters: Staff turnover affects service delivery and creates costs; LGR implementation is a major financial commitment dependent on government direction, creating budget uncertainty
findings.figures: Ringfenced budget allocated for LGR (amount not specified)
findings.quote: Staff retention and recruitment challenges arising from uncertainty associated with LGR, leading to potential loss of skills, knowledge, capacity and organisational resilience.

findings.headline: Full regulatory inspection by housing regulator expected by end of 2026
findings.detail: Under the new Social Housing Regulation Act 2023, the council as a social landlord expects a full inspection by the housing regulator by the end of 2026. Housing team resources are being focused on meeting the requirements of the new act.
findings.matters: New regulatory inspections create compliance costs and potential remediation requirements; failures could result in enforcement action affecting service delivery or costs
findings.figures: Inspection expected by end of 2026
findings.quote: A full inspection by the regulator can be expected by end of 2026

findings.headline: Council scheduled to meet with MHCLG on financial position
findings.detail: The council has scheduled meetings with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government on its financial position as an action within its financial risk management. This indicates direct engagement with central government on financial matters.
findings.matters: Such meetings typically indicate either financial difficulty or significant government engagement on financial support and planning
findings.figures: None provided

findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies homelessness as increasing its financial risk. Actions include pursuing alternative accommodation for homeless people and developing a sustainability plan as part of budget setting for 2027/28.
findings.matters: Homelessness services are a significant and growing cost pressure for councils, directly affecting financial resilience and reserve stability
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Homelessness pressures increase our financial risk.

findings.detail: The council has implemented all audit recommendations from 2024/25. The 2025/26 audit has identified three new recommendations, with management responses detailed in Appendix 1.
findings.matters: External audit follow-through demonstrates whether councils respond to audit findings and strengthen their control environment.
findings.figures: All previous year recommendations resolved; three new recommendations in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: Business Rates Retention Reserve has a funding adjustment draw of £282,651 in addition to £50,709 budgeted usage, totalling £333,360 drawdown
findings.detail: The Business Rates Retention Reserve (opening £743,526) is subject to both budgeted usage of £50,709 and a funding adjustment of £282,651, leaving only £410,167 closing balance. This is a material reduction in a key source of council income flexibility.
findings.matters: Business rates retention is how councils benefit from local economic growth. A significant reduction in this reserve suggests either the council is using reserves to cover shortfalls in retained business rates income, or it has planned a major drawdown to fund expenditure.
findings.figures: Business Rates Retention Reserve opening £743,526, budgeted usage £50,709, funding adjustment £282,651, closing £410,167
findings.quote: Business Rates Retention Reserve (743,526) (743,526) 50,709 282,651 (410,167)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: The £315,000 added to Contingency Reserve matches exactly the £315,000 drawn from LGR Reserve, suggesting either an undeclared transfer or classification inconsistency
findings.detail: Contingency Reserve is being increased by £315,000 (budgeted addition, opening £119,550 to closing £434,550), while LGR Reserve shows an unbudgeted draw of exactly £315,000 from a zero opening balance (closing -£315,000). The identical figure suggests movement between reserves rather than independent budget pressures, but the different classification (budgeted vs unbudgeted) is unusual.
findings.matters: Accounting consistency matters to lenders. If a transfer is being classified as both a budgeted addition and an unbudgeted draw, it raises questions about budget governance, management clarity, and reliability of the forecast.
findings.figures: Contingency Reserve budgeted addition £315,000; LGR Reserve unbudgeted usage £315,000 (exact match)
findings.quote: Contingency Reserve: Budgeted Additions/Useage in 2026/27 (315,000) closing (434,550); LGR Reserve: 0 opening, (315,000) Unbudgeted Useage, (315,000) closing

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: Multiple unbudgeted reserve draws totalling at least £909,588 in 2026/27 indicate forecast errors or budget pressures
findings.detail: The statement shows significant unbudgeted reserve usage across multiple funds: LGR Reserve £315,000; EPR Reserve £131,601; General Fund Reserve £63,987; and broader General Fund Earmarked Reserves showing £520,000 unbudgeted usage. These unbudgeted draws suggest the 2026/27 budget forecast did not hold, and the council is using reserves to cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether these unbudgeted draws represent one-off costs or a structural budget gap. Sustained reserve draws erode financial resilience and indicate a council operating beyond its means.
findings.figures: LGR Reserve unbudgeted usage £315,000; EPR Reserve unbudgeted £131,601; General Fund Earmarked Reserves unbudgeted usage £520,000; General Fund Reserve unbudgeted usage £63,987
findings.quote: Unbudgeted Useage in 2026/27: (520,000) for Total GF Earmarked Reserves; LGR Reserve: (315,000); EPR Reserve: 131,601 as unbudgeted; General Fund Reserve: (63,987)

findings.headline: Gross borrowing revised upward by £1m without explanation
findings.detail: The council's gross borrowing forecast for 2026/27 was revised from £35.683m to £36.683m—a £1m increase (2.8%) compared to the original estimate. The document does not explain the reason for this revision, though it confirms the council will remain within its Capital Financing Requirement and the S151 Officer reports no difficulties foreseen.
findings.matters: An unexplained increase in projected borrowing need may indicate higher-than-expected capital costs or programme changes that warrant clarification when assessing financial sustainability and debt trajectory.
findings.figures: Gross Borrowing: 35,683 to 36,683 (£000s)
findings.quote: Gross Borrowing 35,683  36,683

findings.headline: General Fund reserve buildup cut by 81% as overspends compress planned contributions
findings.detail: The council budgeted to build reserves by £337k in 2026/27 but will now only add £64k—a reduction of £273k (81%). While the absolute reserve balance grows to £1.517m, the ability to strengthen financial resilience is severely impaired.
findings.matters: Inability to build reserves at planned rate indicates the council is consuming financial headroom to balance the current year; slower reserve accumulation reduces capacity to absorb future shocks from homelessness, interest rates, or other pressures.
findings.figures: Budgeted reserve contribution £337k; forecast contribution £64k; variance (£273k); opening reserve £1.453m
findings.quote: The General fund outturn is expected to be a surplus of £64k, as opposed to the £337k surplus that was budgeted for.

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs £92.6k over budget because geopolitical tension delayed interest rate falls
findings.detail: Corporate Management forecasts a £92,600 overspend on debt charges. The paper attributes this to oil market volatility from the Iran conflict preventing interest rates from falling as fast as assumed at budget-setting. The council holds £32.731m gross debt (net £26.831m after cash holdings).
findings.matters: Interest rate assumptions are fundamental to debt affordability; geopolitical shocks forcing revisions demonstrate planning risk and show councils are exposed to external conditions over which they have no control.
findings.figures: £92,600 overspend; £32.731m gross external debt; £26.831m net debt position at 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Volatility in oil markets caused by Iran conflict has prevented interest rates from dropping as fast as assumed when budget was set.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme 42.8% under-delivered with £2.4m slippage driven by capacity constraints on major repairs
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme is forecast at £3.213m against revised budget of £5.622m, with £2.409m slippage. Slippage from the prior year (2025/26) was £905k, higher than expected. The paper explicitly states the remaining shortfall is driven by capacity constraints that have delayed windows and roof replacements—two of the largest repair areas.
findings.matters: Major repairs slippage (roofs, windows) signals the council lacks capacity or resources to execute its repair programme, creating long-term housing stock maintenance risk and potential deterioration liability.
findings.figures: £2.409m slippage on £5.622m budget (42.8%); £905k unplanned slippage from prior year; £803k variance on New Housing Initiatives
findings.quote: The remaining slippage is largely driven by capacity issues, which have delayed progress on the two largest areas; windows and roof replacements.

findings.headline: HRA deficit worsens to £244k and contingency reserve is drawn to maintain minimum balance
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account forecast deficit is £244k against the budgeted overspend of £128k—an additional £116k deterioration. To preserve HRA reserve at the best-practice minimum of 15% of gross income, the council will transfer £281k from HRA contingency reserve. The HRA reserve will close at £687k.
findings.matters: HRA is self-financing from rent income; drawing contingency reserves to meet minimum balance requirements signals cash constraints and reduces the buffer for future housing cost shocks or maintenance emergencies.
findings.figures: £244k forecast deficit (vs £128k budgeted); £281k transfer from contingency; HRA reserve closing at £687k
findings.quote: For 2026/27 the Councils Housing Revenue Account (HRA) net revenue budget was set with a net contribution from reserves of £128k. As at Q1, it is anticipated that there will be a net deficit of £244k, leaving the HRA Reserve at £687k at year end. £281k will be transferred back from the HRA Contingency Reserve to maintain the reserve at a minimum balance equal to 15% of the budgeted gross income for 2026-27.

findings.headline: Emergency accommodation forecast at £164,135 overspend, primarily driven by households issued Section 21 notices and those asked to leave by friends or family
findings.detail: The Built Environment service forecasts £164,135 overspend on emergency accommodation driven by households issued Section 21 notices and those asked to leave by friends/family. The council is mitigating through EARP funding, homelessness prevention, and new posts (Move on Officer, Private Rented Sector Officer), but costs remain elevated above budget.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a demand-led cost that lenders track closely; whether councils are managing the pressure with prevention or being overwhelmed determines financial sustainability. Section 21 evictions are structural—creating a larger pipeline of need.
findings.figures: £164,135 overspend; households issued Section 21 notices and family evictions named as main drivers
findings.quote: Emergency Accommodation expenditure remains above budget due to continued homelessness pressures, with the main drivers being households issued with Section 21 notices and those asked to leave by friends or family.

findings.headline: Local Plan costs exceeding budget; £112k drawn from prior-year grant reserve
findings.detail: Local Plan delivery is £78,550 over budget in year, funded by appropriating £112,550 from a Local Plan grant reserve held from 24/25. The council is using a reserve to fund plan development costs above what was budgeted.
findings.matters: Once the prior-year grant reserve is exhausted, recurring Local Plan costs will need to come from the base budget or creation will stop. This shows planning is under-resourced.
findings.figures: £78,550 overspend, £112,550 from reserves
findings.quote: Appropriation of Local Plan grant received at end of 24/25 to fund additional Local Plan costs over and above reserve movement budgeted.

findings.headline: Finance software upgrade shelved due to LGR; rising costs on legacy system
findings.detail: The council planned to upgrade Integra finance software but shelved the upgrade due to LGR impact. The legacy version is now costing above inflation (£15,480 variation) because the number of remaining users has fallen, spreading fixed costs to fewer licenses.
findings.matters: LGR is deferring investment decisions and creating cost creep on legacy systems. If LGR is delayed or cancelled, the council will be stuck with deferred upgrades and deteriorating software.
findings.figures: £15,480 above-inflation cost increase on Integra
findings.quote: Above inflation increase in costs of Integra due to steady fall in number of remaining users of this particular version. Upgrade to new version had been planned, but was shelved due to impact of LGR.

findings.headline: Licensing team working through backlog of outstanding premises licensing income recovery
findings.detail: The Licensing Section has deployed temporary staff (£51,343) specifically to work through an accumulated backlog of outstanding premises licensing income recovery. This suggests invoices are going unpaid or uncollected.
findings.matters: A growing backlog of collectable income suggests either poor credit control or that premises are not paying, indicating wider business distress in the local area.
findings.figures: £51,343 on temporary cover
findings.quote: Temporary cover to work through backlog of work associated with recovery of outstanding premises licensing income.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit overspend for homelessness at £100k and growing
findings.detail: Housing Benefits forecast shows £100,000 additional cost for non-council tenant rent rebate due to increased expected costs from homelessness. A separate £109,944 shortfall in reimbursement is being recharged to the homelessness budget.
findings.matters: Housing benefit and homelessness costs are reinforcing each other and the shortfall recharge creates circularity. The budget process does not appear to have anticipated this interaction.
findings.figures: £100,000 (increased rebate costs) + £109,944 (shortfall recharge)
findings.quote: Increased in expected costs of Housing Benefit for Homelessness

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility reserve drawn down by £131k for waste staffing
findings.detail: Recycling and food waste collection services are funding additional HGV driver, loader and collector posts from the Extended Producer Responsibility Reserve. This is £65,119 for recycling and £66,482 for food waste, totalling £131,601.
findings.matters: Reserves should absorb one-offs; staffing is recurrent. If waste staffing is permanently higher, the council has a structural overspend and will need to find £130k+ annually or run reserves dry.
findings.figures: £131,601 total (£65,119 recycling + £66,482 food waste)
findings.quote: Costs of additional HGV Driver/Loader posts and two additional Collector/Loader posts. Financed by Extended Producer Responsibility Reserve

findings.headline: Energy market volatility has prevented interest rates from dropping as assumed when budget was set
findings.detail: Debt charges are £94,400 over budget. The paper attributes this to Iran conflict-driven volatility in energy markets, which has kept interest rates higher than expected at budget setting. This is beyond the council's control but shows sensitivity to external markets.
findings.matters: External cost pressures on debt are a leading indicator of whether the council's spending plan was realistic. Unexplained interest rate rises eat reserves or force service cuts.
findings.figures: £94,400 forecast variation on debt charges
findings.quote: Volatility in energy markets caused by Iran conflict has prevented interest rates from dropping as fast as assumed when budget was set.

findings.headline: Unbudgeted business rates now charged on two car parks and Coombe Park property
findings.detail: Two car parks and the Coombe Park property were previously unrated but are now subject to business rates of £29,994 and £20,715 respectively. The council is funding both from business rates retention reserve, not from savings.
findings.matters: Previously unrated assets suddenly becoming rateable is a one-off shock that can recur. It shows the council did not budget for it and must draw reserves to absorb it, indicating cash forecasting weakness.
findings.figures: £29,994 (car parks) + £20,715 (Coombe Park) = £50,709 total
findings.quote: Business rates due to two car parks being previously unrrated - to be funded from business rates retention reserve

findings.headline: Emergency accommodation spending £350k over budget due to homelessness pressures
findings.detail: The council forecast emergency accommodation expenditure £350,000 above budget because of continued homelessness, driven by Section 21 notice issuances and people asked to leave by family. The paper forecasts reduction later in the year through prevention work and pilot schemes, but demand remains structural.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a structural cost pressure with no easy exit and unpredictable demand. A lender assesses whether the council can absorb this and whether prevention measures actually work.
findings.figures: £350,000 forecast variation
findings.quote: Emergency Accommodation expenditure remains above budget due to continued homelessness pressures, with the main drivers being households issued with Section 21 notices and those asked to leave by friends or family.

findings.matters: Allocated capital being deliberately left unspent raises questions about either overbudgeting, project delays, or inability to execute planned works; significant figure in a small council's programme.

findings.matters: Underfunding mandatory compliance work suggests either budgeting error or inability to deploy resources against legal obligations, both relevant to lender assessment of governance and regulatory compliance.

Both are explicitly deferred with preparatory work to follow over the next year, moving substantive work to 2028/29. This is £550k of planned maintenance pushed out two years.
findings.matters: Housing stock condition matters to lending risk; deferring structural maintenance (roofs, windows) signals either cash constraints or reprioritization, and extends the period assets remain unrepaired.

findings.quote: No plans to undertake these replacement works in 2026/27. Over the next year plans will be developed and preparatory work undertaken to establish the replacement programme with a view to carrying out the replacement works from 2028/29 onwards.

Multiple projects show substantial shortfalls: new housing initiatives £803k under, decent homes work £905k under, fire safety £117k under, damp & mould works £70k under.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this represents sound capital management, delivery constraints, or cash pressure affecting the council's investment in its housing stock.

findings.matters: A small reserve addition relative to identified financial pressures indicates the council has limited financial headroom to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.

findings.matters: Unanticipated legal costs in housing stock indicate either governance weaknesses or undiscovered problems with the council's housing assets that could trigger further costs.

findings.matters: Demand-led service costs that the council must meet create uncontrollable budget pressure; unchecked growth in homelessness spending can quickly absorb reserves.

findings.headline: Interest rates causing higher than anticipated borrowing costs
findings.detail: The council identifies rising interest rates as a main financial challenge, causing borrowing costs to exceed budget assumptions. This is one of three pressures putting strain on council balances. No mitigation strategy is detailed.
findings.matters: Higher than anticipated borrowing costs indicate either the council carries significant debt or that market conditions are deteriorating faster than budget planning assumed, reducing financial headroom.
findings.figures: No amounts specified

findings.headline: £50K in legal fees from disrepair and property damage claims against the housing stock
findings.detail: Estates Management has overspent by £100,175, of which £50K is attributed to legal fees arising from disrepair and property damage claims. This indicates the council is defending claims relating to the condition of its rental properties, signalling potential maintenance issues within the housing stock.
findings.matters: Disrepair claims expose the council to financial and reputational liability, suggest capital maintenance backlogs, and indicate housing stock condition that affects both the value of the HRA asset and future repair spending
findings.figures: £50K legal fees; Estates Management overspend £100,175
findings.quote: £50K legal fees related to disrepair and property damage claims.

findings.paper_title: Question on Notice - Direct Debit Council Tax Demands
findings.headline: Council tax demand error with delayed notification to senior management and S151 Officer
findings.detail: An error occurred in council tax direct debit demands. A second demand containing the same error was issued to taxpayers before the S151 Officer, senior management, or councillors were informed of the problem. The question criticises the communication failure.
findings.matters: Council tax collection is a critical and predictable revenue stream; errors in demand processing combined with communication breakdowns between front-line staff and senior finance/governance indicate internal control weaknesses that affect cash flow certainty.
findings.figures: None provided in the question
findings.quote: Why weren't the S151 Officer/senior management and Councillors informed of the error before the second demand was sent out?

findings.headline: 15 audit actions from prior years and 6 from 2025/26 remain open and unimplemented
findings.detail: Audit recommendations agreed in 2024/25 and earlier remain open, with SWAP planning to follow them up again in 2026/27. This pattern indicates the council is slow to implement audit findings and management recommendations.
findings.matters: Slow or failed implementation of audit actions signals weak governance discipline; lenders rely on councils acting promptly on identified control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 21 open actions across two years
findings.quote: 15 agreed actions from 2024/25 remain open (raised by 360), and 6 remain open from 2025/26

findings.headline: Elections audit found Returning Officer claims not reconciled to Payroll & Creditor Systems
findings.detail: The audit found that Returning Officer claims were not being reconciled to the council's Payroll & Creditor Systems, a fundamental control failure. A separate review of payments to permanent Elections staff was also required, suggesting payments were being made without proper verification.
findings.matters: Failure to reconcile supplier payments is a core financial control; it means the council cannot account for where payments have gone, a direct concern for lenders evaluating the council's financial stewardship.
findings.figures: 3 agreed actions from Elections audit
findings.quote: Failure to reconcile Returning Officer claims to the Payroll & Creditor Systems

findings.headline: Transparency Agenda audit found extensive non-compliance with the Local Authority Transparency Code, receiving Limited assurance
findings.detail: The audit identified non-compliance both on the public website and in records. Limited assurance is the second-worst rating issued, and the audit resulted in 7 agreed actions. This reflects a significant governance gap in the council's compliance and transparency controls.
findings.matters: Transparency code compliance is a statutory requirement; non-compliance exposes the council to challenge and indicates weak governance oversight that lenders depend on.
findings.figures: 7 agreed actions from Transparency Agenda audit
findings.quote: A variety of areas on the public facing website were non-compliant with the Local Authority Transparency Code 2015

findings.headline: Anti-fraud report still outstanding and not yet submitted to Audit Committee
findings.detail: The governance framework identifies 'Ant-Fraud Report to be submitted to Audit Committee' as an outstanding area for improvement. Anti-fraud training has been rolled out and policies are in place, but the annual report on anti-fraud progress has not yet been provided.
findings.matters: Lack of a current anti-fraud assurance report suggests the council may not have a comprehensive view of fraud risk or may not be proactively monitoring for fraud.
findings.figures: Anti-fraud training rolled out; Anti-fraud and Anti-corruption policies in place but report outstanding
findings.quote: Anti-fraud policy updated April 2023 and Anti-corruption policy in place. Anti-fraud training has been rolled out across the Council. Annual Report on anti-fraud progress to be provided to Audit Committee

findings.headline: Local Government Ombudsman found fault in homelessness services and council paid financial redress
findings.detail: The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman concluded an investigation and found fault in the council's handling of a homelessness matter. The council was required to issue an apology and provide financial redress, both of which were implemented.
findings.matters: Ombudsman findings indicate the council failed in statutory duties and had to compensate a resident, flagging potential broader service delivery weaknesses.
findings.figures: 1 Ombudsman investigation concluded with fault finding
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman concluded one investigation concerning the Council and found fault in relation to a homelessness matter. As the complaint related to the Council's statutory homelessness functions, rather than its role as a social landlord, jurisdiction rested with the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman rather than the Housing Ombudsman (below). The Ombudsman recommended an apology and financial redress, all of which were implemented by the Council.

findings.headline: Housing Ombudsman found maladministration in disrepair and asbestos information; council issued £600 compensation
findings.detail: The Housing Ombudsman completed one investigation into the council's housing services and identified two maladministration findings: one relating to disrepair and one relating to failure to provide asbestos information. The council was ordered to pay £600 in compensation and provide additional support to the tenant.
findings.matters: Housing service failures expose the council to financial liability and reputational risk, and indicate underlying service delivery or compliance weaknesses in a major council function.
findings.figures: £600 compensation payment ordered
findings.quote: In 25/26, the Housing Ombudsman completed one determination into the Council's Housing Services, which resulted in three findings: two maladministration findings relating to disrepair and the failure to provide asbestos information, and one service failure relating to complaint handling. A total of three orders were issued, including a formal apology, a £600 compensation payment, and a recommendation to provide additional support regarding the housing application and rehousing options.

findings.headline: Financial management governance rated 'Fair' rather than 'Good', indicating improvements still needed
findings.detail: The governance framework review assessed 'Ensuring financial management supports both long-term achievement of outcomes and short-term financial and operational performance' as 'Fair'—meaning satisfactory but improvements are required. This is a core financial management function.
findings.matters: A 'Fair' rating on financial management governance suggests the council's financial control environment has gaps that need addressing before it can be considered robust.
findings.figures: One of multiple governance functions rated Fair (not Good)
findings.quote: Ensuring financial management supports both long-term achievement of outcomes and short-term financial and operational performance. Fair.

findings.headline: Ongoing savings targets required to balance the Medium-Term Financial Plan, with a Sustainability Plan needed to close budget gaps
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has 'resources necessarily limited' and 'ongoing savings targets will be required to balance the Medium-Term Financial Plan.' The 2026/27 budget approval required a 'Sustainability Plan for closing budget gaps' and the council committed to not using General Reserves to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Structural budget gaps requiring ongoing savings targets indicate the council is under financial pressure and may struggle to fund commitments or invest in services without finding new income or making cuts.
findings.figures: MTFS adopted with Sustainability Plan; 2026/27 budget approved with commitment not to use General Reserves
findings.quote: The Council has a good track record of financial management and internal control, but resources are necessarily limited, and ongoing savings targets will be required to balance the Medium-Term Financial Plan.

findings.headline: One external audit recommendation from prior years remains in progress, not yet completed
findings.detail: Of four follow-up recommendations from previous audits, three have been completed but one is still in progress. This indicates a slower-than-desired pace of addressing prior audit findings and potential underlying control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Incomplete prior-year audit recommendations suggest weaknesses are not being resolved and could accumulate into material control failures.
findings.figures: 1 of 4 follow-up recommendations from prior audits still in progress
findings.quote: The report also identified a follow-up of 4 recommendations from previous audits. Out of these 4 recommendations three have been completed with one in progress.
