findings.detail: Grant Thornton's December 2025 audit findings report on 2024/25 accounts included 11 recommendations, with seven classified as medium risk and four as low risk. Management has responded to each, but the number and severity of medium-risk findings suggests material control gaps.
findings.matters: Medium-risk audit recommendations reflect deficiencies in financial controls or compliance that could affect the reliability of accounts or expose the council to material risk.
findings.figures: 11 total recommendations; 7 medium risk, 4 low risk
findings.quote: In December 2025 Grant Thornton issued their Audit Findings Report, covering the audit of the Council's 2024/25 financial statements. Eleven recommendations were identified within the report; seven medium risk and four low risk.

findings.headline: One internal audit returned Limited assurance, below the Reasonable or Substantial benchmark
findings.detail: Of five internal audits in 2025/26, one returned 'High Limited' assurance—the lowest category. This indicates significant gaps or weaknesses in that audit area that require improvement to effectively manage risks. The other four audits returned Substantial or Reasonable assurance.
findings.matters: Limited assurance audits indicate control weaknesses in specific council functions that could expose the council to operational or financial risk.
findings.figures: 1 out of 5 audits rated Limited assurance; 2 rated Substantial, 2 rated Reasonable
findings.quote: For 2025/26 out of a total of 5 audits, 2 returned High Substantial, 2 returned High Reasonable and 1 returned High Limited.

findings.headline: Finance system upgrade deferred with £80k unspent pending local government devolution policy clarification
findings.detail: Finance System Upgrade project had an approved budget of £80,000 with £0 spent. The council notes 'Necessity of upgrade being examined in the light of local government devolution', indicating finance system investment is on hold pending clarity on potential structural and governance changes.
findings.matters: Finance system capability is fundamental to financial management. Deferring planned system upgrades pending policy uncertainty suggests the council is not prioritising finance function modernisation. For lenders, ageing finance systems deferred during a period of governance uncertainty creates questions about financial data quality and management information robustness.
findings.figures: £80,000 budgeted; £0 spent
findings.quote: Necessity of upgrade being examined in the light of local government devolution

findings.headline: New statutory damp and mould remediation programme only 55% spent against legal obligation deadline
findings.detail: Works to address damp and mould issues under new legislation had a budget of £113,952 with only £62,964 spent by year end (£50,988 underspent). The programme includes improved ventilation systems, insulation and damp proofing works. This represents statutory compliance obligations, not discretionary maintenance.
findings.matters: Statutory damp and mould remediation duties cannot be indefinitely deferred. Incomplete spend against this legal obligation represents deferred compliance costs and potential regulatory enforcement risk. For lenders, indicates potential for unexpected future costs if remediation work cannot be deferred further.
findings.figures: £113,952 budgeted; £62,964 actual (55% spend rate); £50,988 underspent
findings.quote: Works associated with duty under new legislation to rectify damp and mould issues. Improved ventilation systems, insulation and damp proofing etc.

findings.headline: Housing maintenance contractor delays: door replacement 93% underspent, entry systems 88% underspent
findings.detail: Two major housing stock maintenance programmes show systemic delivery delays. Front and rear door replacement for Chartwell and Churchill Close (5 blocks, £355k budget) has only £24k spent with 'Phase 1 (30 doors) complete as at 31/03/26', and contractor was not appointed until October 2025. Housing block door entry system replacement for 20 blocks (£308k budget) shows only £37k spend with 'Phase 1 (3 blocks) completed as at 31/03/26', with contractor appointed February 2026. Both projects show 6-12 months of contractor mobilisation delays.
findings.matters: These are ongoing maintenance programmes on existing housing stock. Extended delays deteriorate housing condition and tenant experience. For lenders, the pattern across multiple projects suggests either workforce shortage, supply chain constraints, or project management capacity issues that affect the council's ability to deliver scheduled capital work.
findings.figures: Door replacement: £355,411 budgeted, £24,421 spent (93% underspent); Entry systems: £308,238 budgeted, £37,178 spent (88% underspent)
findings.quote: Door replacement programme for 5 blocks - Chartwell and Churchill Close. Contractor appointed in October 2025. There then followed a period of mobilisation. Phase 1 (30 doors) complete as at 31/03/26.

findings.headline: Fire safety compliance works budgeted at £418k with only £85k spent and contractors not yet appointed
findings.detail: Fire safety compliance work on communal schemes and blocks had an approved budget of £418,873 but actual spend to 31 March was only £85,172 (80% underspent, £334k variance). The document notes that 'subsequently appropriate contractors to be appointed to carry out the works', indicating substantial remedial work identified in fire risk assessments remains uncommenced. This represents a statutory compliance obligation.
findings.matters: Fire safety remediation is a regulated obligation. Incomplete fire risk assessment remedial works create regulatory exposure and potential enforcement action. For lenders, incomplete compliance obligations represent unexpected cost and liability risks, particularly if deferral extends into 2026-27.
findings.figures: £418,873 budgeted; £85,172 actual (80% underspent); £333,701 variance to forecast
findings.quote: Compliance work to communal schemes and blocks to implement remedial works identified in the fire risk assessments. Subsequently appropriate contractors to be appointed to carry out the works.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme £2.26m underspent against £3.83m budget, with 59% slippage to 2026-27
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account capital expenditure to 31 March 2026 totalled only £1.57m against a £3.83m approved budget. The council forecasts £2.26m of this slippage will carry forward to 2026-27, principally from new housing initiatives (£1.12m underspent), door replacement programmes (£331k underspent), fire safety works (£334k underspent), and door entry system upgrades (£271k underspent). This represents a 59% underspend rate.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery at this scale indicates either planning underestimation, execution capability gaps, or resource constraints. For lenders assessing capital structure and capacity, this level of slippage across an entire revenue account's capital programme raises questions about project delivery confidence and whether budgeted investment will materialise as forecast.
findings.figures: £3,834,188 budgeted; £1,570,746 actual to 31/3/26; £2,263,442 slippage to 26/27 (59% of budget)

findings.headline: Debt and treasury management: net debt of £30.4m; £218k interest received on investments in year
findings.detail: The council's total external debt is £35.8m (PWLB and local authority borrowing), offset by £5.4m in temporary investments, giving net debt of £30.4m. Interest received on investments was £218k in 2025/26 (up from £165k in 2024/25), showing benefit from higher interest rates. No treasury management non-compliance reported.
findings.matters: Net debt of £30.4m is sustainable given the council's revenue budget, but the homelessness overspend and capital slippage suggest the council should not take on new long-term borrowing without addressing structural budget issues first.
findings.figures: Total gross external debt £35.778m; investments £5.4m; net debt £30.378m. Interest received £218,427.
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, the total debt portfolio of the Council (including HRA debt) was £35.8m offset by investments of £5.4, resulting in an overall net debt position of £30.4m.

findings.headline: Selective Property Licence Scheme income delayed: £93.8k expected in 2026/27 instead of 2025/26
findings.detail: The scheme has grown to the point where capacity constraints mean the council cannot deliver the forecast income in-year. The report expects £93.8k (26% of the budgeted £360k) to slip into the next financial year. This is a scheme-dependent revenue stream, not a core fee.
findings.matters: Income volatility from a single scheme indicates reliance on discretionary revenue that may not be reliable year to year. The capacity constraint also suggests the council is resourced at or beyond its operational limit for this area.
findings.figures: Scheme forecast income £266k; budget £360k; variance £93.8k (delayed to 2026/27 due to 'increased size of scheme and capacity constraints')
findings.quote: Increased size of scheme and capacity constraints has resulted in £93K of forecast income being delayed until 26/27

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £3.2m on a £7.2m budget; New Housing Initiatives delayed by £1.117m
findings.detail: The capital programme is 45% underspent, with slippage across both General Fund and HRA. The largest single delay is the New Housing Initiatives scheme (£1.117m), which the report notes is delayed because 'further development options are being investigated'. This suggests either cost pressure or scope uncertainty. Other delays cite contractor issues and capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Capital slippage of this scale (nearly half the programme) delays service and housing delivery, and constrains the council's ability to invest in its own asset base. A scheme under active review for 'further development options' may have cost escalation risks.
findings.figures: General Fund capital slippage £938k (28% of £3.364m budget). HRA capital slippage £2,265k (59% of £3.835m budget). New Housing Initiatives slippage £1,117k.
findings.quote: The outturn for the HRA capital programme is £1.570m with slippage of £1,117k due to a delay on the New Housing Initiatives scheme, as further development options are being investigated.

findings.headline: General Fund shifted from budgeted £136k surplus to £63k deficit
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a surplus of £136k; it is now forecasting a £63k deficit. This swing of £199k means the General Fund is no longer delivering a buffer and is drawing on reserves instead of building them. While the position improved £236k from Q3, the direction has moved from positive to negative.
findings.matters: A council expected to break even or build reserves but instead drawing them down is a reversal in financial trajectory. General Fund reserves are now £1.477m, modest for a council of this size.
findings.figures: Budgeted surplus £136k; forecast outturn deficit £63k; swing of £199k. Opening General Fund balance £1,540,066; closing £1,477,248.
findings.quote: The General fund outturn is expected to be a deficit of £63K as opposed to the £136k surplus that was budgeted for.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation is driving an unbudgeted £1.046m overspend
findings.detail: The Built Environment service is £841k overspent, nearly all from homelessness. The council cites S21 evictions, care leavers, and hospital discharges as drivers. Critically, it identifies that statutory rent allowance rates are not keeping up with actual rented property costs in the area, creating a structural gap between what the council must spend and what it is funded to spend.
findings.matters: This is not a temporary budget miss but a mismatch between statutory allowances and market reality. The council cannot control the demand (S21 evictions, hospital discharges) or the allowance rates, so this overspend will recur and grow.
findings.figures: £1,046,822 overspend on homelessness; council-wide General Fund overspend is £257k, so homelessness is 407% of total overspend
findings.quote: Increase in demand for temporary accommodation. Primarily caused by S21 evictions, care leavers and hospital discharges. Pressures caused by statutory rent allowance rates not keeping up with cost of rented property.

findings.headline: Council is currently exceeding the prudential limit for short-term borrowing due to capital slippage delaying long-term refinancing
findings.detail: The council's borrowing maturity structure currently exceeds the revised prudential limit for debt maturing within 12 months. This breach occurred because planned long-term borrowing at the end of 2024/25 was negated by capital expenditure slippage in the HRA (£2,075K). The council plans to remedy this through £2M of PWLB borrowing in Q4 25/26.
findings.matters: Prudential limit breaches indicate that the council's financial planning or forecasting has diverged from reality. Even temporary breaches signal potential management attention gaps or changing circumstances that lenders monitor as indicators of financial discipline and control.
findings.figures: £2,075K HRA capital slippage; £2M PWLB borrowing planned for Q4 25/26
findings.quote: While the Council is currently exceeding the limit for borrowing under 12 months, this is expected to be temporary. New long-term borrowing had been planned towards the end of 24/25, but capital slippage negated the need for it.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: General Fund Capital Receipts Reserve increased to £2.97m with £4.45m in additions
findings.detail: The General Fund Capital Receipts Reserve grew from £358,762 to £2,970,848, with £4,450,000 in additions during the year offset by £1,837,914 in capital spending. This substantial increase in available capital funding is unusual for a council this size.
findings.matters: A sharp increase in capital receipts could indicate one-time asset sales or capital receipts flexibilisation. For a lender, this is important context: it may explain how the council is financing capital schemes, but it also raises questions about whether this is sustainable or a windfall.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts Reserve: Opening £358,762, Additions £4,450,000, Usage £1,837,914, Closing £2,970,848

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve fell by £374,639, reducing emergency headroom
findings.detail: The General Fund Reserve decreased from £1,540,066 to £1,165,427. This £374,639 drawdown represents the council drawing on its contingency reserve to cover in-year spending.
findings.matters: The general fund contingency reserve is the council's buffer against income shortfalls or unexpected costs. A declining balance, especially if part of a trend, signals budget tightness and reduces the council's resilience to further revenue pressure.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve: Opening £1,540,066, Usage £374,639, Closing £1,165,427

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: HRA Revenue Reserve drawn down by £865,964 in the year
findings.detail: The main HRA Reserve fell from £1,758,702 to £892,738, a drawdown of £865,964. This reduction indicates that HRA operational income and expenditure did not balance in 2024/25 without resort to reserves.
findings.matters: A declining HRA reserve in a single year could be timing; but if sustained, it shows the housing service is not self-financing. For a lender assessing HRA viability and rent sustainability, this is a key indicator of whether the HRA can meet long-term obligations without subsidy or rent increases.
findings.figures: HRA Reserve: Opening £1,758,702, Usage £865,964, Closing £892,738

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Statement of Movement on Reserves
findings.headline: HRA Major Repairs Reserve closed at only £91,503 after spending £1.96m
findings.detail: The HRA Major Repairs Reserve was drawn down from an opening balance of £555,003 plus £1.5m in funding to a closing balance of just £91,503. The reserve funded £1,963,501 in major repairs spending, leaving minimal headroom for unexpected repair costs or next year's programme.
findings.matters: A major repairs reserve this depleted leaves the HRA exposed to volatility in repair costs and limits the council's ability to respond to urgent housing maintenance. If major repair spending is expected to remain at this level, the reserve will be exhausted and the council will need external funding.
findings.figures: Major Repairs Reserve Balance: Opening £555,003, Additions £1,500,000, Usage £1,963,501, Closing £91,503

findings.headline: Bringing HRA cleaning in-house created a £20K pension lump sum cost in Q3.
findings.detail: Estates management includes a £20K pension lump sum payment resulting from the decision to bring cleaning services in-house. This represents an emerging cost pressure from restructuring, partially offset by £36K vacancy savings.
findings.matters: Service restructuring decisions create pension and staffing liabilities that affect medium-term budget sustainability and cost control.
findings.figures: £20K pension lump sum, £36K vacancy savings, £5K inflationary increases
findings.quote: £20K increase in pension lump sum attributable to HRA due to bringing cleaning in-house.

findings.headline: £870K slippage on New Housing Initiatives capital project is deferring short-term borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Capital charges show a £59,149 underspend variance attributed to slippage on the New Housing Initiatives scheme. The delayed project reduces current-year short-term borrowing and interest costs, though the capital work and its borrowing requirement remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Capital project delivery affects the council's borrowing profile and timing; slippage can indicate execution, governance, or planning issues that push financing needs into future periods.
findings.figures: £870K slippage, (£59,149) capital charges variation
findings.quote: Impact of slippage of £870K related to the New Housing Initiatives capital project on short-term borrowing costs and interest recievable.

findings.headline: £2.075m slippage on HRA capital programme, with £1.082m delayed on New Housing Initiatives scheme under review
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme is forecast to slip by £2.075m against a revised budget of £3.835m. The largest single item, the New Housing Initiatives scheme, has slipped by £1.082m because development options are being reconsidered. Additional slippage is attributed to contractor issues and capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Capital slippage on housing development could reflect either strategic reconsideration or delivery difficulties. A lender tracking the council's ability to execute its housing programme and generate capital receipts would want to understand why a major scheme is being redesigned mid-year.
findings.figures: HRA capital slippage £2.075m; New Housing Initiatives variance £1.082m (from £1.871m budget to £789m outturn)
findings.quote: The outturn for the HRA capital programme is £1.760m with slippage of £2,075k due to a delay on the New Housing Initiatives scheme, as further development options are being investigated.

findings.headline: General Fund balances falling from £1.540m to £1.165m as reserves are consumed to cover overspending
findings.detail: The council forecast a £146k surplus at budget but is now forecasting a £375k deficit—a £521k adverse swing. This £375k deficit is being absorbed from General Fund reserves, reducing them by approximately 24% during the year. The paper states that while most services have been controlled, the council has been unable to fully offset homelessness pressures despite considerable efforts.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion signals reduced financial resilience and the council's inability to absorb future shocks. A fall of this magnitude in one year raises questions about the sustainability of the financial position.
findings.figures: Opening balance £1.540m, closing £1.165m; forecast deficit £375k vs budgeted surplus £146k
findings.quote: The General fund outturn is expected to be a deficit of £375k, as opposed to the £146k surplus that was budgeted for.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation overspend of £645k, caused by S21 evictions and statutory allowance rates falling behind market rents
findings.detail: The homelessness service overspent by £644,959 in the nine-month period, making it the single largest variance in the General Fund. The paper attributes this to increased demand for temporary accommodation driven by S21 evictions (no-fault evictions), care leavers, and hospital discharges. The core problem stated is that statutory rent allowance rates do not keep pace with actual rented property costs in the area, forcing the council to bridge the gap.
findings.matters: A lender would see this as a structural budget problem driven by national policy (S21 reform) and statutory rate-setting outside the council's control. Demand is rising faster than budgets can accommodate, and the root cause shows no sign of resolving.
findings.figures: £644,959 overspend; Homelessness service was £1.782m forecast vs £1.205m budget
findings.quote: Increase in demand for temporary accommodation. Primarily caused by S21 evictions, care leavers and hospital discharges. Pressures caused by statutory rent allowance rates not keeping up with cost of rented property.

findings.headline: New Housing Initiatives programme forecasts 49% slippage from 2025/26 into 2026/27
findings.detail: The largest capital scheme (2025/26 approved budget £1.77m) shows £870k forecast slippage. The programme then continues at £2.2m for 2026/27 and remains at £1.2m-£2.2m annually through 2030/31. Five-year funding is £4.17m from reserves and £937k from borrowing.
findings.matters: Slippage of nearly 50% on the council's primary new initiative in a single year signals either unrealistic original planning or execution challenges. For a lender, this raises questions about delivery capacity and whether housing targets will be met as planned.
findings.figures: 2025/26 approved budget £1,772,499; forecast slippage £870,687; 2026/27 budget £2,213,400; reserve funding £4,168,082; borrowing £937,354

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy (2026/27) & Treasury Management Indicators (2026/27 - 2030/31)
findings.headline: No new long-term General Fund borrowing planned despite rising capital programme demands
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges the need for long-term borrowing as part of a 'mix,' but forecasts explicitly state 'No new long-term borrowing is forecast on the general fund over the next five years.' Yet short-term borrowing rises to £12.5m, suggesting capital needs are being met entirely through refinancing existing debt.
findings.matters: This creates a mismatch between stated strategy (need for long-term debt) and actual plan (no new long-term borrowing). Lenders should understand whether this reflects constrained access to long-term capital, resource limitation, or execution risk on the strategic shift.
findings.figures: No new long-term borrowing forecast; short-term debt rising from £9m to £12.5m
findings.quote: No new long-term borrowing is forecast on the general fund over the next five years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy (2026/27) & Treasury Management Indicators (2026/27 - 2030/31)
findings.headline: Forecast debt reduction for 2025/26 depends on completing two major property sales
findings.detail: The General Fund short-term debt forecast of £9m in 2025/26 is contingent on capital receipts from the sale of Bushloe House and Oadby Pool. If either sale is delayed or falls through, borrowing requirements would increase.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are uncertain; if property sales stall or underprice, the council would need either additional borrowing or spending cuts. This creates contingent risk for the medium-term forecast.
findings.figures: £9m forecast dependent on Bushloe House and Oadby Pool sales
findings.quote: Short-term debt applicable to the General Fund is forecast to drop to £9m during 2025/26 due to the anticipated capital receipts from the sale of Bushloe House and Oadby Pool.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy (2026/27) & Treasury Management Indicators (2026/27 - 2030/31)
findings.headline: HRA forced to refinance maturing debt into long-term borrowing to maintain prudential ratio limits
findings.detail: The original £18.114m HRA self-financing settlement debt has been repaid at £1m per annum and refinanced with short-term borrowing. From end of 2025/26, this must switch to long-term borrowing to maintain short-term debt below 50% of gross debt. Planned refinancing: £2.0m (25/26), £1.0m (26/27), £2.0m (27/28), £2.6m (28/29), £1.1m (29/30), £0.6m (30/31).
findings.matters: Shows HRA debt management is now constrained by prudential rules, not choice. The council must refinance to longer-term borrowing on a fixed schedule, reducing flexibility.
findings.figures: £18.114m original HRA debt, £1m per annum repayment, new refinancing schedule
findings.quote: This repayment has been refinanced with short-term borrowing to date, however as from the end of 2025/26, it will be necessary to refinance using new long-term borrowing, in order to maintain the proportion of short-term borrowing to gross debt below 50%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy (2026/27) & Treasury Management Indicators (2026/27 - 2030/31)
findings.headline: General Fund short-term borrowing forecast to rise 39% over five years
findings.detail: After an anticipated drop to £9m in 2025/26 (from capital receipts), General Fund short-term debt rises steadily to £12.5m by 2029/30 and 2030/31. This increases refinancing requirement and rate exposure.
findings.matters: Rising short-term debt indicates capital programme demands and increases annual refinancing need. Combined with stated refinancing risk concerns, this is the exact exposure the council says it needs to reduce.
findings.quote: Total external short-term borrowing relating to the General Fund for future financial years is expected to be: 2025/26 £9.0 million, 2026/27 £10.5 million, 2027/28 £11.0 million, 2028/29 £12.0 million, 2029/30 £12.5 million, 2030/31 £12.5 million

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy (2026/27) & Treasury Management Indicators (2026/27 - 2030/31)
findings.headline: Council shifting strategy: eight years of short-term borrowing now recognized as carrying refinancing risk
findings.detail: After avoiding long-term borrowing entirely from 2016/17-2024/25 and relying on short-term rates to manage costs, the council now explicitly recognizes this creates unacceptable refinancing exposure. The treasury strategy states the need for future borrowing to be 'a mix of short and long-term debt.'
findings.matters: A fundamental shift in treasury approach suggests either capital programme demands are straining the cost model or interest rate environment has changed risk calculus. For lenders, it flags the council's previous strategy was no longer tenable.
findings.figures: No long-term borrowing 2016/17-2024/25; new strategy calls for mix going forward
findings.quote: While there is scope to continue with this policy to some extent, the need to control the council's exposure to refinancing risk means that future borrowing in support of the capital programme will need to consist of a mix of short and long-term debt.

findings.headline: Uncommitted pension fund deficit of £7.5m to be paid from future revenue
findings.detail: The council has a pension fund deficit valued at £7.5m that is committed to future payments, in addition to £34.7m current debt. This will require ongoing revenue funding and could constrain budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Uncommitted liabilities reduce financial headroom and could impact ability to absorb future shocks
findings.figures: £7.5m pension deficit
findings.quote: the Authority is committed to making future payments to cover its pension fund deficit (valued at £7.5m)

findings.headline: HRA housing investment programme of £2.2m per year for new schemes with HRA debt rising to £21.5m
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is investing £2,213k per year in new housing schemes plus £2,504k in other capital works. This ongoing program is driving HRA debt upward from £20.188m to £21.463m by 2030/31, requiring careful management of rental income and cost recovery.
findings.matters: Sustained HRA investment is capital-intensive and requires viable business planning; the underlying viability of the housing programme is not detailed here
findings.figures: £2,213k new schemes, £2,504k other works (2026/27); HRA debt rising to £21,463k by 2030/31
findings.quote: HRA capital expenditure is therefore recorded separately and includes the building of new housing schemes (£2,213k), and other capital works per the HRA Business Plan (£2,504k).

findings.headline: Large one-off asset sale of £5.926m from Bushloe House and Oadby Pool reduces future capital funding
findings.detail: The council is receiving £5.926m in capital receipts in 2025/26 from asset sales to fund the General Fund capital program entirely and reduce debt. Capital receipts then drop to £0.255m per year thereafter, a cliff that will require the council to rely on revenue funding and borrowing for future capital projects.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's future capital funding capacity and whether asset disposals are strategic or indicate financial pressure
findings.quote: The General Fund CFR is expected to decrease by £0.379 during 2026/27, due to the capital program being funded entirely from capital receipts accruing from the sale of Bushloe House & Oadby Pool.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: New regulatory inspection regime (Regulation of Social Housing) driving unbudgeted staffing costs
findings.detail: Three new posts are being added to HRA staffing specifically to meet the new Regulation of Social Housing inspection requirements: Asset Management and Information Officer, Housing Inspector for Damp and Mould, and Compliance Assistant. This represents a £210k increase in HRA employee expenses.
findings.matters: New regulatory requirements can shift service costs unexpectedly; this shows the council has not yet absorbed this cost into baseline expectations
findings.figures: HRA employee expenses increase of £210k for 2026/27
findings.quote: These posts are required due to work related to the Regulation of Social Housing inspection.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Leicestershire business rates pooling arrangement ending, removing historic financial benefit
findings.detail: The council has benefited from business rates pooling since 2013/14, retaining growth that would otherwise be subject to levy. This pooling arrangement is now ending from 2026/27 onwards due to the reset of the Business Rate Retention Scheme, eliminating this advantage.
findings.matters: A lender assessing forward income stability needs to know when external funding arrangements change
findings.figures: Retained Business Rates 2026/27 £1,941,252 (compared to £2,434,256 in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Leicestershire Councils have collectively decided that business rate pool will not operate in from 2026/27 onwards.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Capital programme dependent on completion of two specific asset sales that have not yet closed
findings.detail: Capital bids totalling hundreds of thousands were received but without identified funding sources. The council plans to fund them through capital receipts from the sale of Bushloe House and Oadby Pool. If these sales do not complete, the capital programme would require prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if capital investment plans have confirmed funding or are contingent on asset sales that may not happen
findings.figures: Capital programme across General Fund and HRA involving multiple schemes including £2.213M New Housing Initiatives, £2.330M Decent Homes Works
findings.quote: It is intended that they will be financed from capital receipts expected from the sale of Bushloe House and Oadby Pool.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account running a deficit that is worsening and drawing down reserves
findings.detail: HRA budget shows a £128k deficit for 2026/27, which is £57k worse than 2025/26, to be met from the HRA reserve. HRA reserve declining from £1,674,678 to £1,157,222 by March 2027. The MTFP shows surplus only from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: A lender tracking HRA sustainability needs to know if it is dependent on reserve depletion or if it is self-sustaining from rental income
findings.figures: 2026/27 deficit £128k (£57k higher than 2025/26); HRA reserve closing balance £1,157,222 by March 2027
findings.quote: The budget for 26/27 is £128k deficit which is £57k more than 25/26. This will be met from the HRA Reserve.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Large budget gap problem from 2023/24 was only recently resolved
findings.detail: The council's 2023/24 external audit identified significant recommendations around large budget gaps and financial sustainability. The 2024/25 audit marks improvement with no significant weaknesses identified, but this recovery is recent and the prior distress was serious.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a council was in serious financial distress 18 months ago and whether the apparent recovery is sustainable
findings.figures: 2023/24 had 'recommendations regarding the large budget gaps in the MTFP'; 2024/25 found 'no significant weaknesses'
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Auditors Annual report has identified no significant weaknesses with our financial sustainability, and has one improvement recommendation in terms of addressing any future budget gaps. This is a significant improvement on the 2023/24 report which had recommendations regarding the large budget gaps in the MTFP

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation planned for April 2028 creates medium-term uncertainty
findings.detail: A government invitation in February 2025 requires the council to prepare proposals for unitary reorganisation, with shadow authority elections in April 2027 and vesting day (merger) on 1 April 2028. Until then, the council continues as-is, but strategic planning and continuity are clouded by this structural change.
findings.matters: A three-year countdown to dissolution creates uncertainty for lending, long-term planning, and service continuity. The council's financial trajectory through 2028 is now shadowed by institutional change.
findings.figures: Full plan submission deadline 28 November 2025, vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: This would mean that Oadby and Wigston Borough Council would cease to be a council on the 31 March 2028, and would be merged into the new unitary council as from the 1 April 2028, referred to as the vesting day.

findings.headline: External borrowing of £35.4m includes £19.5m short-term borrowing beyond prudential limit headroom
findings.detail: Total borrowing is £35.4m (£15.9m long-term plus £19.5m short-term) against a prudential code limit of £46m. While within limits, the short-term borrowing of £19.5m is described as being 'in lieu of long-term debt', indicating ongoing external financing needs for cash management rather than capital projects.
findings.matters: Substantial borrowing, particularly short-term debt standing in for long-term funding, suggests ongoing liquidity pressure and dependence on external funding to smooth cash flow.
findings.figures: £15.871m long-term borrowing, £19.506m short-term borrowing, prudential limit £46m, headroom £10.6m
findings.quote: Additionally, there is another £19.506m of short-term borrowing, both for cash flow purposes, and in lieu of long-term debt.

findings.headline: Structural constraint on revenue growth: dense housing and size limit council tax and business rates expansion
findings.detail: The borough is already built to capacity with limited land for new housing, which prevents growth in council tax base through New Homes Bonus or business rates retention. This geographic and physical constraint removes a primary lever other councils use to grow revenues.
findings.matters: Unlike growth-oriented councils, Oadby and Wigston cannot grow its way out of deficits. Revenue growth is capped by planning constraints, forcing reliance on service cuts or asset sales.
findings.figures: 58,000 residents in nine square miles (dense urban borough)
findings.quote: The Council's is severely restricted by its size and existing housing density. The Borough therefore has a limited capacity to host additional housing compared to most other districts and boroughs. This means the Council has limited capacity to increase its funding by growing its Council Tax base and attracting New Homes Bonus and is also limited in attaining Business Rates growth.

findings.headline: Housing Benefits overspent by £660k in 2024/25, the largest single budget variance
findings.detail: Housing Benefits is the single largest adverse variance on the General Fund, driven by cost-of-living pressures increasing demand for housing support. The narrative links this to 'unprecedented demands around homelessness support and costs' from inflation's impact on residents.
findings.matters: Housing-related support is a demand-led, partially uncontrollable cost that is growing due to external economic conditions, compressing available resources for other services.
findings.figures: £660,256 adverse variance on Housing Benefits
findings.quote: The impact of inflation on the cost of living creates more demand for our services and is creating unprecedented demands around homelessness support and costs.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan projects deficits each year with reserves insufficient to bridge them
findings.detail: The MTFS approved in February 2025 shows budget gaps projected across the 5-year forecast, with the General Fund reserve depleting over the period. The council explicitly recognises that reserves cannot continue to balance the budget going forward and will become inadequate to handle external shocks.
findings.matters: The council faces a multi-year structural deficit requiring service cuts or significant revenue generation beyond current levels. Reserves provide little cushion.
findings.figures: 5-year MTFS period, opening General Fund reserve £1.540m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Council recognises that the reserves cannot be used to bridge budget gaps going forward and that the depletion of reserves means the Council will become unable to respond to external financial challenges.

findings.headline: General Fund deficit of £118k in 2024/25 despite £807k sustainability savings programme
findings.detail: The council overspent by £118k despite implementing significant cost-reduction measures. This came after the General Fund reserve fell from £1.540m opening to £1.422m closing (a £343k reduction in the year). The council is unable to achieve budget balance even with service changes and income generation.
findings.matters: Indicates structural revenue problems: the council cannot absorb its operating costs within its core funding, even with active management intervention.
findings.figures: £118k deficit, £807k savings achieved, £343k reserve reduction, closing reserves £1.422m
findings.quote: The outturn position for the General Fund Revenue Account is a £118K deficit.

findings.headline: No formal documented process for identifying right-of-use assets under IFRS 16
findings.detail: The council completed a completeness review of leases for IFRS 16 implementation but did not formally document this process. The auditor identified that the council did not have a formal process for identifying right-of-use assets. Based on draft financial statements, the council has identified no material right-of-use assets and has only trivial lease liabilities, but the lack of documented procedures creates a risk that significant leases could be omitted.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 requires lease liabilities to be recognised on the balance sheet; undocumented asset reviews create a completeness risk and suggest weak asset capture processes.
findings.figures: No undisclosed material leased or right-of-use assets identified; trivial lease liabilities
findings.quote: We noted that a completeness review of all leases held by the Council was undertaken but not documented for the purposes of IFRS 16 implementation. This increases the risk that significant leases may be omitted from the IFRS 16 assessment.

findings.headline: Two material related party transactions totalling £7,500 were not disclosed, where councillors held directorships
findings.detail: The auditor identified two undisclosed related party transactions totalling £7,500 where council members held directorships in entities that transacted with the council during the year. Although immaterial to the council's perspective, the transactions were material to the related parties. The council has amended its related parties forms to require disclosure of all transactions between the council and entities in which councillors have an interest, regardless of significance.
findings.matters: Incomplete related party disclosures suggest weak processes for identifying conflicts of interest and monitoring connected transactions; this is a governance control that lenders rely on.
findings.figures: £7,500 in undisclosed related party transactions
findings.quote: We noted two undisclosed related party transactions totalling £7,500, where councillors held directorship in entities which had transacted with the Council in the period. Although these transactions are not material from the Council's perspective, they are considered material to third party.

findings.headline: Depreciation on building assets calculated using incorrect useful economic lives, not in line with council policy
findings.detail: Testing identified instances where the useful economic lives of assets used to calculate depreciation were not consistent with the council's accounting policy. For two building assets and council dwelling acquisitions, depreciation was calculated using inaccurate useful economic lives, resulting in a £63,000 adjustment to the cost of services and £837,000 to HRA expenditure. The council is to review asset useful economic lives as part of an overall asset register review.
findings.matters: Systematic depreciation errors indicate weak controls over asset accounting and risk that PPE balances are misstated; total impact was £900,000 across CIES lines.
findings.figures: £63,000 adjustment to general fund; £837,000 adjustment to HRA expenditure
findings.quote: on recalculation of the annual depreciation charge for the Council's property plant and equipment we identified for two building assets and council dwelling acquisitions that depreciation had been calculated using an inaccurate useful economic life and not in line with the Council's accounting policy.

findings.headline: Audit identified £739,000 in adjustments to the financial statements, with £124,000 impact on useable reserves
findings.detail: The auditors identified three categories of adjustments: depreciation on council dwellings and buildings totalling £837,000 (due to incorrect useful economic lives); a net pension fund liability adjustment of £309,000 related to IFRIC 14 asset ceiling assessment; and audit fee disclosure corrections. These adjustments had a net impact of £739,000 on the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement and £124,000 on useable reserves.
findings.matters: Material audit adjustments to both reported results and reserves indicate deficiencies in financial statement preparation controls and accounting estimates.
findings.figures: £739,000 adjustment to CIES; £124,000 impact on useable reserves; £837,000 depreciation adjustment; £309,000 pension adjustment
findings.quote: We have identified three adjustments to the financial statements that have resulted in a £739,000adjustment to the Council's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. The impact on the level of the Council's useable reserves is £124,000.

findings.headline: £2,305k of fully depreciated property, plant and equipment could not be verified as existing; £1,117k has been written off
findings.detail: The council identified £2,305k of assets recorded at nil net book value in the fixed asset register. A verification exercise found that assets totalling £1,117k had been disposed of or could not be located and were removed. The council does not have a formal annual process to verify asset existence, creating a risk that recorded assets no longer exist. The auditor also noted £835k of fully depreciated intangible assets.
findings.matters: Unverified assets inflating the balance sheet indicate weak asset management controls; written-offs of £1,117k suggest either poor record-keeping or untracked disposals.
findings.figures: £2,305k of fully depreciated PPE; £1,117k derecognised; £835k of fully depreciated intangible assets
findings.quote: the Council does not have a formal process to verify the existence of assets held at year end. We identified £2,305k of fully depreciated VPE and £835k of fully deprecated intangible assets. Management have made an in year adjustment to derecognise assets which could not be verified.

findings.headline: Key finance staff departures have forced the S151 officer to both create and approve journals, breaching segregation of duties
findings.detail: Due to key finance team members leaving the organisation, the S151 officer was required to approve journals that should have been approved by other officers. Journals can also be created and approved by the same individual where another member posts the journal. This creates a segregation of duties risk. The council has amended its journal policy to require different officers to create and approve journals.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties in transaction approval is a basic control; its breakdown signals staffing strain and control environment weakness, both relevant to lending risk.
findings.figures: Only three officers can approve manual journals
findings.quote: the S151 officer has approved journals. This has not been the case for the full period, however, was required due to key finance team members leaving the organisation. This may cause a segregation of duties risk and reduce the integrity of the review process.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Draft Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Draft Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income (£875k) has no confirmed continuation beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: The budget includes £874.972k from Extended Producer Responsibility funding in 2026/27. The council explicitly states there is no information confirming this income continues beyond that year. If this stream lapses, it would need to be offset by spending reductions or other income sources, materially worsening deficits already forecast in 2027/28 and beyond.
findings.matters: Loss of £875k annual revenue would amplify existing MTFP deficits; a known material income stream with no continuation certainty is a balance-sheet risk
findings.figures: £874,972 EPR income in 2026/27; no continuation information available
findings.quote: There is currently no information on Extended Producer Responsibility beyond 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Draft Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Draft Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Three new housing posts (£211k cost) mandated for social housing regulation compliance
findings.detail: The HRA budget adds three new positions: Asset Management and Information Officer, Housing Inspector – Damp and Mould, and Compliance Assistant. These are required to meet the 'Regulation of Social Housing inspection' programme. HRA employee expenses increase by £211k from 2025/26 (£1.177m) to 2026/27 (£1.389m), including these posts plus 3% pay award.
findings.matters: New statutory compliance requirements drive permanent, recurring cost increases that reduce future financial flexibility; housing regulation obligations are expanding
findings.figures: £211k increase in HRA employee costs; three new posts
findings.quote: These posts are required due to the work involved in the Regulation of Social Housing inspection.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Draft Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Draft Capital Programmes
findings.headline: MTFP contains deficits in three consecutive years (2027/28 to 2029/30) with no finalized balancing plans
findings.detail: The medium-term plan shows budget gaps of £36k (2027/28), £55.7k (2028/29), and £100k (2029/30), totalling £192k in unplanned deficits. The council acknowledges these gaps and defers development of balancing plans until after the government settlement. Proposed options include fee increases and invest-to-save schemes, but specific amounts and timing are not specified.
findings.matters: Councils must demonstrate how each year will balance; deferring finalisation of balancing plans creates contingency risk that deficits may erode the opening General Fund balance of £2.556m
findings.quote: Once the Finance settlement is known a more accurate forecast can be presented to ensure that plans are in place to balance these years.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Draft Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Draft Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Revenue budget projections depend on Fair Funding Review settlement not yet finalized
findings.detail: The council's MTFP forecasts a £870k cumulative surplus based on 'indicative announcements' from the Fair Funding Review. However, final allocations remain unknown. The council states it will not have clarity until the provisional settlement is published mid-December. Current figures are estimates pending official confirmation.
findings.matters: If the December settlement differs materially from forecasts, the projected surplus may not materialise and could create additional deficits across multiple MTFP years
findings.figures: £870k cumulative surplus forecast; provisional settlement due mid-December 2025
findings.quote: we will not have full clarity over the exact allocations of funding until the provisional settlement is published in mid-December

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Draft Revenue Budgets, Medium Term Financial Plan and 2026/27 - 2030/31 Draft Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account running £150k deficit, up from £71k, funded from contingency reserve
findings.detail: The HRA draft budget for 2026/27 shows a £150k deficit (compared to £71.4k in 2025/26), an increase of £79k year-on-year. The council plans to fund this deficit from the HRA Contingency Reserve. While the HRA five-year forecast recovers to surplus in years 2-5, this creates an immediate draw on reserves.
findings.matters: Drawing down contingency reserves to cover operating deficits erodes financial resilience; the growing deficit pattern signals structural pressure in housing operations
findings.figures: £150k deficit 26/27, £71.4k deficit 25/26; increase of £79k
findings.quote: The draft budget for 26/27 is £150k deficit which is £79k more than 25/26. This will be met from the HRA Contingency Reserve.

findings.headline: The council relies on £18.5m of annual short-term borrowing in lieu of longer-term financing.
findings.detail: Of the £35.4m total borrowing at 31 March 2025, £19.5m (55%) is short-term (under 365 days). The council undertakes £18.5m of short-term borrowing each year and continuously refinances it upon maturity, rather than locking in longer-term PWLB rates. Short-term borrowing currently costs 4.80%–5.98% compared to long-term rates of 2.66%–4.10%.
findings.matters: Refinancing £18.5m annually at rolling short-term rates exposes the council to interest rate risk. If market rates continue to rise or short-term lending becomes less available, annual interest costs could increase substantially.
findings.figures: £18.5m short-term borrowing undertaken in 2024/25 and 2023/24, total borrowing £35.4m at 31 March 2025, short-term portion £19.5m, short-term interest rates 4.80%–5.98%, long-term rates 2.66%–4.10%
findings.quote: There was £18.5m of short-term borrowing undertaken during 2024/25 (2023/24 £18.5m), in lieu of long-term borrowing.

news_drafts.lead: A finance director at another council would want to observe how peers address slow audit remediation, as consistently overdue actions could indicate governance or organisational capacity constraints affecting financial management.

news_drafts.headline: Three audit findings in Revenues and Benefits remain in pending remediation status with deadlines in December 2026 and June 2027.
news_drafts.lead: A lender would care about unresolved audit findings affecting revenue administration, as revenue collection is fundamental to the council's financial resilience and debt service capacity.

news_drafts.lead: Pension contributions of 22.4% plus fixed costs represent a significant and growing embedded cost in the council's base budget that limits flexibility to redirect spending to emerging priorities
